results.summary: This analog design generates a differential sinusoidal signal at approximately 25 kHz using a digital-to-analog converter and a low-pass filter. It is intended for bio-applications and requires external precision voltage references and an oscilloscope for testing. The design is notable for using standard-cell-based analog techniques, including fully integrated capacitors and ultra-low-voltage OTAs. It operates from a 2.56 MHz clock and provides differential outputs on two analog pins.

This design implements a configurable 32-bit watchdog timer with optional password protection. It features a down-counter that generates a timeout event if not fed, and supports password modes to prevent accidental writes. The design is verified using Cocotb simulation, covering reset, enable, timeout, password, and feed functionality. It requires no external hardware and is intended for integration into larger systems.

This design is a hardware convolutional neural network accelerator that classifies 10x10 pixel images using two 5x5 kernels. It communicates over SPI to load image and weight data, trigger inference, and read results. The design includes a state machine that processes the image in fragments, performs multiply-accumulate operations, and uses max-pooling to produce a classification. It requires an external SPI master for control and data transfer.

This design implements an SPI slave that receives 8-bit data and displays it as a 2-digit hexadecimal value on a multiplexed 3-digit 7-segment display. It synchronizes SPI signals to the system clock and generates a receive valid pulse. The display controller time-multiplexes the digits at approximately 333 Hz. External hardware includes an SPI master and a common-anode 7-segment display.

This design implements a slot machine game with three reels displaying four possible symbols on a VGA screen. The game starts with random flashing symbols, and pressing the start button initiates spinning that stops each reel sequentially. It requires a 25 MHz clock, two push buttons for start and reset, and a Tiny VGA PMOD connected to a VGA monitor. The design is a simple interactive game with no additional external components.

This design is a VGA-based mini-game inspired by Flappy Bird, where the player controls a logo that must avoid scrolling pipes. It includes features such as pause, hard mode, and score tracking, with controls mapped to input pins. The game outputs VGA signals to a TinyVGA PMOD and requires a VGA monitor or simulator. The design is implemented in Verilog and uses a bitmap ROM for the player sprite.

This design displays the MMU Cybertron logo on a VGA screen. It provides inputs to tile the logo across the screen and enable color output. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor. It is a simple visual display project with minimal documentation.

This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen. It includes inputs for tiling, color enable, color index selection, and vertical flipping. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor. It is a simple visual display project with minimal documentation.

This design generates the IEEE logo bouncing around on a VGA screen, with the color changeable via a button. It is a submission to the Open Silicon 2026 workshop and requires a VGA display. The design is simple and uses no external hardware beyond a laptop to run and display the output. The documentation is minimal.

This design implements a single artificial neuron (perceptron) in pure combinational logic. It takes four binary inputs, each multiplied by a 2-bit weight, sums them, and compares the result to a configurable threshold to produce a binary output. Weights and threshold are set via input pins, making it fully reconfigurable without re-synthesis. The design includes a cocotb testbench and requires no external hardware.
